items.title: Money Stuff: They Found Some Walter Victims
items.summary: “No victims” The basic story of Mark Walter and TWG Global, his holding company, is that TWG owns some insurance companies, and those insurance companies would raise money by selling annuities to customers, and Walter would control how that money was invested, and he would lend some of the money to himself to buy sports teams. Insurance regulators have pretty strict rules about related-party transactions, for reasons that are obvious if you think for a minute about the phrase “lend some of the money to himself to buy sports teams.” When an insurance company is lending its boss money to buy sports teams , it is taking different and spicier credit risk than it would be if it were just buying normal bonds of unaffiliated companies. But TWG’s insurance companies would make a lot of those loans through third parties, which would then turn around and lend the money back to TWG’s businesses. And the insurance companies’ financial statements would not count those loans as related-party loans. Eventually federal prosecutors and insurance regulators started asking questions. “After receiving subpoenas, those insurers disclosed more than $20 billion of loans that should have been labeled as affiliated transactions, but weren’t .” Bad. At the same time, though, owning sports teams has been a lucrative business in recent years, and as far as I can tell it has all worked out great? TWG put out a statement in August saying so: Affiliated transactions should be properly disclosed, but to state that they “generally” have the potential to “loot” the insurer is untrue. The reality is that Group 1001 [ the TWG insurance group ] has invested in real assets that are performing well; the insurance companies have recognized significant income from the investments and no policyholders have lost money because of these transactions. The statement also said: “There is no victim here. No one has been harmed, and no one has claimed they were harmed.” I have pondered that claim a few times . It can’t quite be true. If the world had known the true level of the insurance companies’ affiliated transactions, then … something. Something. Like: Insurance regulators would have demanded that the insurance companies have more capital to offset the increased risk of all those affiliate transactions. Ratings agencies would have given the assets lower ratings, and the insurance companies would have responded by having higher capital to preserve their own financial-strength ratings. Ratings agencies would have given the insurance companies lower ratings, and they would have had to pay higher interest rates on the annuities they sold. Financial advisers would have read the disclosures, said “hmm this sounds risky,” and recommended that their customers look elsewhere for annuities, again...

items.title: Money Stuff: Don’t Bet Against the Sports Bets
items.summary: Money Stuff Swaps, chargers, BDCs, Hood, puzzles. Kalshi gaming regulation You know what’s funny? There is a real legal dispute about whether Kalshi and other prediction markets should be allowed to offer sports bets without complying with state gaming laws. Kalshi and the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission take the view that (1) Kalshi is federally regulated by the CFTC, (2) sports bets are “swaps” under federal regulation, (3) federal regulation preempts state gaming regulation, so (4) buzz off, states. Many states disagree, and there has been litigation around the country. (We have talked about this several times .) Two federal appellate courts have sided with the states, but another has sided with Kalshi. The state that lost that last case (New Jersey) is asking the Supreme Court to review it, and last week 39 states filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s request. So did the National Football League . I assume that the Supreme Court will take the case. I have no idea what it will decide. I think this is a tough question, courts have disagreed on the answer, it is all pretty politically charged, the Supreme Court can kind of do whatever it wants, and I have no real model of what it will want. I could not tell you the probability that Kalshi will win and get to continue offering sports bets. So, out of muscle memory, I fire up Kalshi to check that probability. “Supreme Court Will Rule Kalshi Sports Bets Are Legal, Yes/No,” where is it? But Kalshi doesn’t list that contract ! [1] Here’s “ A Kalshi Contract on the Legality of Kalshi Contracts ,” by Joseph Grundfest: This note proposes that Kalshi list a "Kalshi Sports Legality" contract indexed to the outcome of United States Supreme Court litigation addressing whether Kalshi's sports-indexed contracts are federally regulated in a manner that preempts state law. Kalshi has previously listed at least 16 contracts indexed to Supreme Court determinations. No rule or regulation prevents Kalshi from listing the proposed contract. The proposed contract would provide a market estimate of the probability that the Supreme Court rules that Kalshi's sports-indexed contracts are legal. The contract would thereby create valuable hedging opportunities for Kalshi investors. It would also create hedging value for Kalshi customers who might lose access to Kalshi markets. These hedging rationales are more substantial than rationales Kalshi presents to support other Kalshi contracts, such as contracts indexed to parlays or to specific in-game events, such as whether the first play in a football game leads to a touchdown. Money Stuff: Pre-IPO Perpetual Futures Swap ETF
items.summary: Money Stuff MANGOS, prime, longshots, buffet. MANGOS What is the best way to get economic exposure to Anthropic stock right now? There are bad answers ( expensive SPVs , fake SPVs ). Here are two arguably good answers: Just own Anthropic stock. Own perpetual futures on Anthropic stock on Hyperliquid. The first answer is pretty self-explanatory. Anthropic has stock, and people own it, and owning it gives you economic exposure to Anthropic stock. There are problems. Not just anyone can own Anthropic stock. It is a private company, and its shares do not trade on an exchange. You more or less need to get the stock from Anthropic , so this approach requires you to be an employee or a venture capital investor in one of its funding rounds or an effective altruist hedge fund manager . For most of us, that rules out this approach entirely. But there is another problem, even if you can get the stock. The other problem is that Anthropic stock is fairly illiquid. [1] You can’t easily sell it, until it goes public. Owning the stock gives you economic exposure to the stock, but you don’t get to decide how long you keep that exposure. And you don’t really know its price . So you do have economic exposure to the stock — if it goes up, your stock is worth more — but you don’t necessarily know how much. The second answer is weirder. Hyperliquid Labs runs a leading platform for trading perpetual futures contracts. Traditionally perpetual futures are a crypto thing, a way to make levered bets on cryptocurrencies, they have expanded into stocks and commodities. Kalshi launched an S&P 500 futures contract and is working on perpetual futures for individual stocks. Perpetual futures contracts are basically bets on prices: One person goes long, one person goes short, the short pays the long if the stock goes up, and the long pays the short if it goes down. A perpetual futures contract on an individual public stock is just a levered bet on that stock, and by arbitrage it will closely track the price of the underlying stock. If SpaceX stock trades at $167.60, and SpaceX perpetual futures trade at $165, arbitrageurs will buy the futures and sell the stock until the prices are in line, etc. [2] But perpetual futures on private stock have no arbitrage mechanism to make the price correct. If Anthropic perpetual futures trade at $120, while Anthropic’s stock is at $100, arbitrageurs cannot sell the futures and buy the stock until the prices converge: They can sell the futures, but they can’t buy the stock. [3] Also, how do you even know that “Anthropic’s stock is at $100”? Anthropic doesn’t trade liquidly or publicly, so you don’t know its price from minute to minute, the way you know the price of the futures. items.title: Money Stuff: ESG Gets More Illegal
items.summary: Is ESG illegal? US securities laws have rules restricting activist shareholders. The main ones are: If you acquire more than 5% of a company’s stock, and you plan on “ changing or influencing the control ” of the company, you have to promptly file a disclosure on Schedule 13D setting out your plans, your source of funds, etc. If you are a passive investor without any interest in changing or influencing control of the company, you can file a shorter, less detailed Schedule 13G . So if you are an activist hedge fund looking to run a proxy fight, and you go over 5%, you have to file a 13D; if you’re a normal mutual fund, you probably file a 13G. The point of the 13D is to alert the company, and its shareholders, to the fact that an activist is involved in its stock. If you team up with another investor — “when two or more persons act as a partnership, limited partnership, syndicate, or other group for the purpose of acquiring, holding, or disposing of securities of an issuer” — you are considered to be part of a “ group .” If you’re in a group, your shares are added together for securities-law purposes: If you own 3% of the company’s stock, and I own 3% of the company’s stock, and we agree to do an activist campaign together, then we form a group that owns 6% of the stock. So we need to file a joint Schedule 13D, disclosing that we are a group and own 6% of the shares. If you go over 10% of a company’s stock, you are restricted from trading the stock: If you buy stock and quickly sell it at a profit, you might have to give up those profits. (These are the “Section 16 short-swing profit rules .”) If your group goes over 10% of the stock, everyone in the group is subject to short-swing profit rules . This stuff is pretty vague. What does it mean to “change or influence the control” of a company? There are some obvious cases: If you are an activist hedge fund planning to run a proxy fight to replace the board of directors, or a potential buyer planning to launch a hostile takeover offer , you clearly want to change or influence the control of the company and you have to file a 13D. But if you are a regular old mutual fund that would never launch a proxy fight, you still might want to occasionally meet with the managers of the companies whose stock you own. In those meetings, you might ask questions and suggest ideas; you might say “hey I think you should expand the widget business and cut back on the sprockets,” or “man I did not like your last ad campaign,” or “what are you doing about climate change?” Are those efforts to “change or influence the control” of the company? Historically the answer has mostly been no; historically, everyone has assumed that 13D is for classic activists (who wage proxy fights), and that mutual funds can use 13G while still...

items.title: Money Stuff: Mergers and Acqui-hires
items.summary: Reverse acqui-hire In recent years, the US technology industry invented a new kind of mergers-and-acquisitions transaction. Traditionally there were two main sorts of M&A transaction: The acquirer buys the target company , in a merger or stock purchase; the shareholders of the target company get something (cash, acquirer stock) in exchange for their shares of the target, and the acquirer ends up owning the target corporate entity. The acquirer buys the assets of the company, in an asset purchase; the target company gets something (cash, acquirer stock) in exchange for its business. If the target is selling all of its assets, it will be left as an empty shell, and will probably distribute the cash or stock to its shareholders and liquidate. These are both pretty normal transactions, and many rules are set up to treat them similarly. So, for instance, Delaware corporate law requires a shareholder vote for a merger , or for a sale of “all or substantially all” of a company’s assets. US antitrust law requires a “Hart-Scott-Rodino premerger notification report” — where the acquirer tells antitrust regulators about the deal and gives them the opportunity to object — for any acquisition of more than $133.9 million worth of stock or assets. You might get different accounting or tax treatment for different deal structures, but many of the big-picture effects are the same however you structure the deal. The antitrust part is important. The big tech companies are very big, there is a lot of political and regulatory worry that they are monopolists, and there is at least some winner-takes-all flavor to the AI race. Meta or Alphabet or Nvidia might really want to do a $20 billion AI acquisition here or there, but that might be risky from an antitrust perspective. So they’re in the market for ways to do acquisitions without, technically, doing acquisitions. Many early-stage artificial intelligence startups consist mostly of (1) people and (2) ideas. The startup has some AI researchers, and they’ve come up with some model or harness or chip design or robot or whatever, and it’s pretty promising. But the startup doesn’t have, like, a giant portfolio of data-center real estate, or a robot assembly line, or a bunch of customer contracts. If a big tech company wants to acquire a startup like that, it could buy it in a merger, or buy all of its assets. But the new structure is: The acquirer hires the target’s employees, or most of them, or at least the people who are critical to its valuable ideas. The acquirer gets a waiver, from the target’s board of directors, allowing it to do all that hiring. I came across some beautiful chanterelles at Uwajimaya while filming our Japanese Pantry Guide the other day, and while I normally make this pasta dish with much less expensive mushrooms, I love chanterelles enough that I couldn't resist. The good news is that the specific mushroom really isn't important here. Button or cremini mushrooms work great. So do shiitake, portobello, hen of the woods, oyster mushrooms, or virtually any mixture you can find at the grocery store or farmers market. The important part is giving the mushrooms enough heat and time to actually brown them before you start building the sauce. This is one of those pastas where the sauce doesn't really exist until the very end. You start by browning the mushrooms hard in olive oil (I like to throw in a thyme or rosemary sprig while the mushrooms sauté and fish it out later), then add a little onion or shallot and garlic.
